votes.rationale: PMF lens only: who already pays cash for THIS job. D7 wins because I re-fetched it — swiftvalues.co.uk sells the identical artifact ("£99 Probate Valuation, HMRC-compliant, online in 48 hours", photos-in/s.160 PDF-out, human-fulfilled, self-serve checkout) against 65,099 gov.uk-sourced quarterly applications; that is a same-job price, same buyer, same deliverable. D11 next: medsolercm.com live-confirms "Credentialing Service Starting At $99 Per Insurance Credential" for exactly this labor, and CAQH's 120-day re-attestation makes demand structurally recurring. D5 third: tabulera.com confirms $399/mo Starter for <500 employees (same job, software) plus Beneration selling it as a 5-day human service; its 5%-error and 89%-auto-clear figures are vendor marketing and I discount them. D1's job is priced only bundled inside $6.5–8.5k flat fees, and its headline anchor is adjacent — I fetched counselpro.ai: $499/matter, practice areas bankruptcy/family/estate/probate, Medicaid and elder law absent. D9 rests on Rastro's $1,000/mo same-job AI plus adjacent data-pool/authoring fees. D8, D13, D6, D10 all cite adjacent-market prices: D8's $0.06–0.15/lot is for prose descriptions, not the number; D13's $5–$379 spread is the redaction verb but its buyer count is unsourced by its own admission; D6 prices inspection software, never the coding layer; D10's $200–500/route (TransitWiki, confirmed) is real but competes with a free, human-supported RTAP builder. D3's paying buyer is enterprise, its target buyer uses free Presidio; the $20–35k Tonic figure is a Vendr third-party estimate, not a vendor page. D12's only prices come from SEO consultancy pages I distrust. D4 is refuted by its own evidence: clientconflictcheck.com is $199–249/YEAR against a $99–499/MONTH hypothesis. D2 has no fetched same-job price at all — pure cost-avoidance inference, with CMMC Phase 2 suspended.

Ranked purely on how hard a $20/mo assistant or an agentic browser can eat this by 2027-08. Top of the list is where the generalist is legally barred, not merely inconvenient: D2's input is CUI, and DFARS 252.204-7012 plus the Dec-2023 FedRAMP-equivalency memo make pasting it into ChatGPT the prohibited act itself — plus 40,000 local files and a marking register, none of which a browser can reach. D1 has no legal bar but the largest patience-proof workload on the ballot: 600 degraded fax pages, deterministic penalty arithmetic against 51 staggered divisors a generalist is silently stale on, output as an XLSX exhibit filed with a state agency. D9 is the purest "machine-checkable acceptance test" shape — 10k SKUs against a 5,500-class ETIM taxonomy emitting XSD-valid BMEcat a data pool accepts; patience does not converge on that. D3 is strong (PHI, folder scale, cross-corpus pseudonyms) but its wall is softer than D2's: institutional BAAs with Microsoft/OpenAI already exist, and Presidio sets the floor at zero. D4/D13/D5/D8 all hold one strong lever — private persistent graph, zero-transmission file surgery, recurring cross-month ledger, proprietary realised-price index. Bottom: D11/D12 sit in the agentic-browser bullseye (Skyvern already sells generic self-serve carrier-portal automation at $149/mo — that refutation is live, not hypothetical); D6 and D10 are patience-solvable (voice + 1M context over 71 public HUD PDFs; a chat-plus-validator loop for a 3-route feed); D7 is a one-shot consumer job a browsing assistant can approximate. Distrusted: D7/D8's entire moat rests on LiveAuctioneers/the-saleroom terms the miner admits it never audited; D11's "no anti-automation clause we could find" is absence-of-evidence; D4 cites help.clio.com while noting it returned 403; identical "free local tools colonised face-blurring" boilerplate in D2 and D3 signals miner templating, not independent checking.

AP3 lens only. Top three own a corpus whose labels are free because reality already wrote them, and a fine-tune that is forced rather than chosen. D13: CourtListener public-domain substrate (Public Domain Mark, quarterly regen) with identifiers injected at known character AND pixel spans — it manufactures a labelled distribution (PII after bad OCR) that exists nowhere in the wild; the fine-tune is mandatory (bytes may not leave), and the harness becomes a per-document guarantee via the re-read-your-own-output pass. D2: DTIC/SAM.gov markings self-label, and DFARS 252.204-7012 (fetched) bars the generalist outright — moat by prohibition. D4: RECAP docket party tables auto-label unstructured filings, giving a self-renewing held-out RECALL number. Distrusted claims: D1 concedes "until the eval harness says yes... the moat is only the rule corpus" — a rule corpus of published divisors is a knowledge base, refuted by the cycle-3 pivot. D6 is the clearest failure: 30–50k paraphrases generated BY Claude from 71 public PDFs is distillation, and a distilled approximation cannot beat its teacher; the ToS question on that is never raised. D3's harness is legally compromised — n2c2 is DUA-gated and may bar commercial use, so it cannot certify against the standard benchmark. D7/D8 hold the ballot's only genuine market secret (realised hammer prices) but both admit LiveAuctioneers/the-saleroom terms are unaudited — assembly legality unresolved. D12 says outright the card dies if carrier ToS clearance fails. D10's harness and corpus are both public and free, so nothing accrues. Unflagged across D2/D3/D13: browser-shipped weights are extractable from cache.

I re-fetched platform.claude.com pricing: Haiku 4.5 $1/$5 ($0.50/$2.50 batch), Sonnet 5 $2/$10 ($1/$5 batch — the page now states the $3/$15 rise "will not occur"), Opus 5 $5/$25, batch 50%, cache read 0.1x; caniuse confirms WebGPU 85.56%, Firefox off by default; Gemini Flash-Lite $0.10/$0.40 ($0.05/$0.20 batch). Every AP4 figure on the ballot checks out; D7/D8 used $3/MTok Sonnet, so their margins are understated, not inflated. D1 leads despite being cloud-native: $2-5 against $199/file is 97-99%, its own stated worst case (no fine-tune, all Sonnet) still clears 94%, pricing is per-unit so COGS tracks revenue, and it is the only card that prices its cost tail (750-page cap, $0.20/page over). It also honestly refuses a WebGPU claim it can't support — 600 scanned pages is not a browser workload. D3/D13/D2 are ~100% by construction and immune to price moves; I order them by browser honesty: a 150M int8 encoder (D3) is genuinely fast in-tab, a 150-400M q4 tagger (D13) nearly so, whereas D2's three-model 400-900MB bundle sweeping 40,000 files is the claim I most distrust — feasible in principle, days of tab-time in practice, and a forced cloud fallback would erase the whole margin thesis. D5 (97-99%, two verified providers, cache at 0.1x) and D4 (prepaid $199-499 indexing fee recovering batch cost) hedge well. I discount D6's 809M Whisper-turbo on a phone GPU and D8's "amortised infrastructure" dodge for an always-on retrieval GPU. D11 (70% worst case, 33-60% on overage) and D12 (16-50% on the Agency tier, and no API-price risk stated at all) are the only fragile margins here.

Ries lens only: how few weeks to a charged card, and how soon the buyer's next reason to buy arrives. D5 wins because the pipeline is a frontier VLM over invoice PDFs plus embedding blocking — the "fine-tuned cross-encoder" is deferrable to v2 (the card already routes residual pairs to a frontier call) — the demand event repeats every single month, and the free single-invoice audit returns a dollar number that is self-evidently right or wrong. Its named friction is real: two inputs, and the card itself flags "census exports obtainable from every small HRIS" as unproven. D9 and D10 both ship v1 on a frontier API with a deterministic assembler and an external validator (XSD / Canonical GTFS Validator) as a free, objective acceptance test — the cleanest MVPs here — but D10's buyer converts a feed once and then goes quiet, so it drops. D1 explicitly states margin holds "even if we never ship the fine-tune", and one state plus one divisor is a shippable v1 against an RFV deadline. D6 has the lowest input friction on the ballot (talk into a phone) and a v1 of Whisper-API + 71 public standards in context; the fine-tune and WebGPU mode are pure v2. D13's local tagger is nominally mandatory but deterministic recognizers carry most of it; the flagged glyph-deletion/rasterize spike and $15/mo ticket cost it. D7/D8 must scrape and calibrate a 500k-2M-lot comparables index before any defensible number exists — corpus-before-first-dollar, on unaudited LiveAuctioneers terms the card admits it did not read. D11/D12 are authed third-party portal automation, the most brittle build here. D3 and D2 are the worst on this lens: both bar the frontier API by construction, so a fine-tune plus a WebGPU bundle must exist before dollar one, and D2's demand event was deflated by the July 2026 CMMC Phase 2 suspension.

Judging only by smallest whole product. D13 Blackbar is the minimum viable machine on every axis: one input (a PDF), one output (a redacted PDF), no per-state corpus (FRCP 5.2/HIPAA identifier list is fixed), and its card explicitly rejects the extension path ("no Chrome Web Store... dodges store review"); its named hard part (glyph deletion) already carries a rasterize fallback — the textbook 20% that ships. D10 Feedwright has one canonical output schema with a binary pass criterion (validator zero errors) and no jurisdictional variance. D6 Walkcode has the narrowest input surface on the ballot (audio we ourselves capture) against a single federal taxonomy of 71 standards; its WebGPU "local mode" is optional scope by its own risk note. D7/D8 share one deliverable each (item schedule / one CSV row per lot) and single-jurisdiction or no-jurisdiction scope, but both hang on a scraped realised-price index whose ToS both cards admit are unaudited — that hidden corpus machine, not the UI, is why they sit below D6. D5 is a clean two-file-drop web app but doubles the parsing surface (arbitrary carrier layouts plus arbitrary HRIS census exports) and adds a stateful retro-credit ledger. D3 spans notes, PDFs and spreadsheets with 18 classes; D1 is a plain web app but three output artifacts across 51 divisors with staggered effective dates; D9 is worst on output multiplicity (four recipient profiles plus ETIM release migrations) over a taxonomy of thousands of classes. D2 scans 40k mixed files including CAD via three local models plus an air-gapped bundle; D4 needs six integrations. D12 and D11 are last on the stated criterion — MV3 plus store review plus brittle third-party portal wizards, and D11 adds fifty state Medicaid portals and a 200-field schema.

Only one candidate literally hands the buyer money on run one: D5 PremiumDiff, where the incumbent itself publishes the finding rate (Beneration: ~5% of premium in error, $100k/mo spend → ~$5k/mo found) against a fetched price floor (Tabulera $399/mo, demo-gated) — $99-199/mo to recover thousands monthly is a self-evident, recurring, evidence-anchored delta. D1 has the best ceiling-vs-labor ratio: $199/file against CounselPro's fetched $499/matter and a paralegal-week buried inside a $6.5-8.5k committed flat fee; the budget is already spent, we just capture it. D9's budget is the most literally documented in cash already leaving the account (2BA €2,150-5,070/yr, ETIM-Mapper's live price API €1,228-8,647/yr, Rastro $1,000/mo) and we price at a tenth. D11 rides a forced 120-day re-attestation clock against a fetched $99/payer human price. D2 has the ballot's cleanest arithmetic ($1,788/yr vs ~$21,900/yr of GCC High seats at a fetched $65.20/user/mo) but the fetched 13 July 2026 CMMC Phase 2 suspension guts the forcing function and the saving is hypothetical scope the buyer may already have bought. D7 undercuts a fetched £99+VAT human price but cannot sell the signature and HMRC guarantee that £99 actually buys; its 80%-overvalue claim is a vendor assertion, flagged. Distrusted: D12's 65-min→12-min study and $2,500-30,000 project prices come from vendor-SEO sites, not primaries. Bottom four fail pricing power outright — D4 asks 12x the only fetched self-serve anchor ($199/YEAR) with no forced budget; D3 fights free MIT Presidio for grad-student labor; D13 is a $15 ticket with an unsourced buyer count; D10 admits free funded substitutes, PO buyers and one-shot purchase.

Traction lens only: does a machine stand where the buyer already hurts? D11 has the most complete stack — a Chrome Web Store listing against uncontested queries ('CAQH autofill'), a free NPPES-roster-mismatch checker that is programmatic, self-maintaining and diagnoses the problem for the buyer, a 120-day re-attestation clock as a dated recurring hook, presence inside the form itself, and dense named communities (r/CodingandBilling, credentialing groups). D5 wins on trigger cadence: the invoice arrives monthly, the free one-invoice audit returns a dollar figure, and 'billed for terminated employee insurance' is a pain phrase currently answered only by demo-gated vendor blogs. D7 sits on ~250-260k E&W grants/year with 93% filed digitally (MoJ, fetched) — a dated, high-intent consumer search plus a self-generating category price index; demerit is one-off purchase. D6's 71 parsed NSPIRE standards give a textbook pSEO surface with a free lookup and a 1 Feb 2027 forcing date. D2's no-upload checker is the only wedge a DFARS-paranoid buyer will try, and SAM.gov/RPO lists are genuinely enumerable — but the 13 Jul 2026 Phase 2 suspension gutted the urgency the channel depends on. D12 mirrors D11 with thinner free surfaces. D13 has the lowest activation friction on the ballot but the most contested SERP (iLovePDF/Smallpdf/Adobe) and $15 ARPU. D4's Clio marketplace is a real store, undone by 10-100GB corpus indexing before first value. D1 I distrust most: its proposed SEO surface is medicaidplanningassistance.org — its own cited source, an entrenched incumbent — and the free wedge demands a client's bank statements. D9/D3/D10 have tight bullseyes but thin query volume, a free-Presidio/RTAP floor, and slow link-building rather than channels.

Judging only recurrence, roster/portfolio expansion, and data-driven switching cost. D11 leads: CAQH/DataSpring re-attestation is a forced 120-day clock per provider "regardless of whether anything changed" (card, fetched medsolercm/dataspring evidence), the billing unit is applications that scale with the shop's provider roster and payer count, and the stated lock-in — "switching cost is the vault" of 400 provenance-tagged records — is the deepest customer-side accumulation on the ballot. D5 is next: the carrier invoice arrives every month forever, tiers scale with covered lives and broker groups ($12/group beyond 25), and the month-over-month retro-credit ledger is genuine continuity lock; I discount it slightly because value per cycle may decay after the first ghost-employee cleanup, and the card concedes customers who never convert findings to credits won't renew. D4's entity graph plus cleared/escalated decision log is the best switching-cost story of all, and screening recurs at every intake with seat tiers by attorney count — held at 3 only because the purchase is risk-avoidance the card itself calls a "nobody got fired for Ctrl-F" sale. D12 (renewal cycle + hundreds of submissions/month) and D6 (8-15 units/day, per-unit tiers) recur heavily but accumulate little the customer would lose. D1 recurs monthly per firm but each case is independent. D9/D10 are episodic (release migrations; 2-4 service changes/year, with hosting the only subscription reason). D2/D3/D13 are locally-resident by design, so nothing accumulates anywhere — D3 is grant-cycle bursty, D13 competes with free at $15/mo. D7 is explicitly one-shot ("LTV is a single £39"); its only recurring buyer, the trade tier, is unproven. Distrusted: D6's inspector-population gap, D11's unvalidated ICP count, D12's unresolved carrier ToS.

AP5 lens only: incumbent naming quality, fetched prices, and whether the gap is a real empty flank or the incumbent's next pricing tier. D1 leads: 4/5 priced (Relaw $269/$349, CounselPro $499/matter, Estateably $179/$198, DocuClipper $20/$111/$360), it names CounselPro as "the real threat," and I confirmed counselpro.ai live — $499/matter, six practice areas, zero Medicaid/look-back — so the gap is a different statutory deliverable, not a tier. I distrust its decisive "no tool does this" citation: that is Relaw's own marketing blog. D2's flank survived my own search (only enclaves/managed services at $8-25k), but only 1/5 has a fetched price and it isn't a competitor. D4 earns credit for chasing phantom vendors (deepknit.ai) and reporting the negative; D8 has the ballot's best price density but sells a scoreboard over a feature Estimint/AuctionWriter already ship, at 2-4x their price. D9 overstates Rastro: it publishes a free ETIM Classification Checker and developer APIs — Classfile's free wedge, occupied — plus undisclosed ETIM licensing risk that killed the ACES/PIES sibling. D5 falls hard: tabulera.com says Starter is for under-500-employee firms, $399/mo, 30-day trial, self-service — so the "gap" is one tier below a published tier. D10 competes with free FTA-funded RTAP; a sibling died for exactly that. D12's only priced incumbent is Skyvern ($29/$149) already marketing carrier-portal automation. D13 is last and should be struck: it claims "every incumbent below is a server" while its own sibling rejection fetched SafeRedact (browser-local, $12/$29-mo) the same day. I verified live — SafeRedact processes locally, plus RedactProof ("redacted directly on your own hardware"). Neither appears anywhere in the file.

Judging only A3 + the arbiter remnant: how the design carries wrong-output risk unattended. D1 leads because its two highest-consequence outputs (completeness grid, penalty divisor arithmetic) are deterministic code, every flagged line carries an image crop and page number, sub-threshold items land in a separate "unresolved" schedule outside the exhibit, staleness is displayed rather than silently used, and poor coverage aborts before billing. D2 has the ballot's best epistemic framing — "absence of an indicator is not evidence of non-CUI", designation authority disclaimed to the Government, low-confidence rows excluded from any settled count, an unprocessed-files appendix — with FCA-grade consequence. D13's round-trip verifier (re-read the produced file, refuse export) is the strongest single mechanism here, but I distrust its "per-document guarantee" framing: the same detector that missed a span on input misses it on output, a correlated blind spot the card underplays. D9 and D10 earn place by making acceptance machine-checkable (XSD/recipient profile; the canonical GTFS validator in-loop) with blank-not-guessed fields — though validator-clean is not value-correct in either. D11/D12 optimize the right asymmetry (wrong-fill rate, blank beats wrong, never press Attest/Submit); D12 drops for admitted unresolved carrier-ToS and coverage-voiding E&O. D4's never-issue-a-clearance stance, published recall and nightly lower-threshold re-sweep are textbook. D3 blocks export until review — but a confidently-missed identifier never enters that queue, and its recall rests on unvalidated synthetic-to-real transfer. D6's refund trigger measures abstention (>20% uncoded), not correctness, which rewards over-coding, atop unproven ASR-plus-quantized-classifier accuracy. D7 last: a tax-facing figure, an unsigned pack displacing a signed one, and a citation trail built on an explicitly unaudited scraping ToS.

AP6 only: what can a counterparty revoke while nobody is watching? D10 wins because its highest-consequence dependency, the Canonical GTFS validator, is Apache-2.0 and vendorable, GTFS is a community spec, and the API layer costs <$2/feed. D9 verified best-in-class: I fetched etim-international.com/classification/license-info and the model genuinely is ODC-BY, free, commercial-use, attribution-only; member-gating hits only the official validator, which the card already routes around via the published XSD. D13 owns its weights, dodges the Web Store deliberately, and CourtListener bulk data is confirmed public-domain, regenerated quarterly. D1 quantifies its price shock ("~$10-12/file against $199" on frontier-only) — the strongest tolerance on the ballot; Haiku batch $0.50/$2.50 verified. D5's two-provider parsing is good but a BAA constrains failover to labs it holds one with. D4 depends on Clio/PMS APIs that can delist. D3/D6/D2 share verified browser exposure (WebGPU 85.56%, Firefox unsupported; showDirectoryPicker is "Limited availability / Experimental", Chromium-only). D6 sits behind a date HUD has now moved three times (to 1 Feb 2027, FR 30 Sept 2025). D2 is worse than its card admits: DoD suspended Phases 2, 3, 4 and "all future implementation milestones" with no new date, and officials declined to rule out ending the program — though DFARS 7012 and the LOGZONE FCA settlement do keep a floor. D11 improves on its card — I fetched the CAQH PDP terms and found no anti-automation clause plus explicit Practice Administrator sanction — but Web Store limited-use policy, unresolved per-payer terms and silent DOM breakage remain. Bottom three fail on fetched terms: LiveAuctioneers §8.3 bars "any robot, spider, scraper" and derivative works; the-saleroom 3.2(c) bars database-building "by spidering or otherwise" — that is D7's and D8's entire moat, and both misquote Sonnet 5 input at $3 where the page says $2, so "fetched today" is doubtful. D12 self-declares the kill switch: unfetchable, non-uniform carrier portal terms it admits could kill the card.
